newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's De Benedetti faces fresh indictment bid.
newsitem.headline: Italy's De Benedetti faces fresh indictment bid.

text.p: Italian prosecutors have asked for entrepreneur Carlo De Benedetti to be sent to trial for alleged corruption and illegal political party funding, judicial sources said on Friday.
They said De Benedetti, former chairman of hi-tech group Olivetti , was among 45 businessmen and politicians against whom Rome magistrate Giuseppe Pititto was pressing charges.

Others included former prime minister Bettino Craxi of the defunct Socialist Party and the former administrators of the Christian Democrat and Italian Communist parties, Severino Citaristi and Renato Pollini.
No date was immediately set for the committal hearing.

Investigations began in 1992 into whether contracts awarded by Italy's state railways to various party-linked cooperatives involved the transfer of funds which were then covertly paid to political parties.

The sources said Pititto alleged Olivetti had paid a senior Transport Ministry official several hundred million lire (tens of thousands of dollars) for inside information on railway projects so that the company could prepare services to offer.
Pittito alleges that the money was then channelled to political parties, the sources said.

Lawyers for De Benedetti, who has other graft cases pending, issued a statement which said the contributions were paid in 1987 and 1988 and that their client had reported the payments of his own accord to anti-graft investigators in 1993.
The statement said the payments took place "in the context which we know existed that obliged companies, in order to survive, to submit to methods of this kind".
Milan's "Clean Hands" team of magistrates began exposing entrenched graft in public life in 1992.
The resultant Tangentopoli (Bribesville) scandal brought down Italy's old political guard including Craxi, now living in self-imposed exile in Tunisia.
Many businessmen implicated in the scandal have argued that pressure was exerted on them to pay political parties bribes or risk being denied lucrative public works contracts.
